[2023 spring ms probability — problem 3]

A box has 3 yellow and 2 red balls. Flip a fair coin: heads $\Rightarrow$ sample 2 balls with replacement, tails $\Rightarrow$ without replacement. Let $Y$ = number of red balls obtained. (1) Distribution of $Y$. (2) $\mathbb{E} Y$. (3) $P(\text{first ball red} \mid \text{second ball red})$. (4) $P(\text{sampled with replacement} \mid Y = 2)$.

response.text:
Let \(H\) denote heads = “sample with replacement,” and \(T\) denote tails = “sample without replacement.” We have

\[
P(H)=P(T)=\frac12.
\]

There are \(2\) red balls and \(3\) yellow balls.

---

## (1) Distribution of \(Y\)

Conditional on \(H\), the two draws are independent with red probability \(2/5\), so

\[
Y\mid H \sim \operatorname{Binomial}\left(2,\frac25\right).
\]

Thus

\[
P(Y=0\mid H)=\left(\frac35\right)^2=\frac9{25},
\]

\[
P(Y=1\mid H)=2\left(\frac25\right)\left(\frac35\right)=\frac{12}{25},
\]

\[
P(Y=2\mid H)=\left(\frac25\right)^2=\frac4{25}.
\]

Conditional on \(T\), the sampling is without replacement, so \(Y\) has a hypergeometric distribution:

\[
P(Y=k\mid T)=\frac{\binom{2}{k}\binom{3}{2-k}}{\binom{5}{2}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P(Y=0\mid T)=\frac{\binom20\binom32}{\binom52}
=\frac3{10},
\]

\[
P(Y=1\mid T)=\frac{\binom21\binom31}{\binom52}
=\frac6{10},
\]

\[
P(Y=2\mid T)=\frac{\binom22\binom30}{\binom52}
=\frac1{10}.
\]

Using the law of total probability,

\[
P(Y=k)=\frac12 P(Y=k\mid H)+\frac12 P(Y=k\mid T).
\]

Hence

\[
P(Y=0)=\frac12\cdot \frac9{25}+\frac12\cdot \frac3{10}
=\frac{33}{100},
\]

\[
P(Y=1)=\frac12\cdot \frac{12}{25}+\frac12\cdot \frac6{10}
=\frac{27}{50},
\]

\[
P(Y=2)=\frac12\cdot \frac4{25}+\frac12\cdot \frac1{10}
=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

So the distribution of \(Y\) is

\[
\boxed{
P(Y=0)=\frac{33}{100},\quad
P(Y=1)=\frac{27}{50},\quad
P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
}
\]

---

## (2) \(\mathbb E[Y]\)

Using the distribution from part (1),

\[
\mathbb E[Y]
=0\cdot \frac{33}{100}+1\cdot \frac{27}{50}+2\cdot \frac{13}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb E[Y]
=\frac{27}{50}+\frac{26}{100}
=\frac{54}{100}+\frac{26}{100}
=\frac{80}{100}
=\frac45.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[Y]=\frac45.}
\]

---

## (3) \(P(\text{first ball red}\mid \text{second ball red})\)

Let \(R_1\) be the event that the first ball is red, and \(R_2\) the event that the second ball is red. We want

\[
P(R_1\mid R_2)=\frac{P(R_1\cap R_2)}{P(R_2)}.
\]

Now \(R_1\cap R_2\) is the event that both balls are red, i.e. \(Y=2\). From part (1),

\[
P(R_1\cap R_2)=P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

Also, regardless of whether sampling is with or without replacement, the marginal probability that the second ball is red is \(2/5\). Hence

\[
P(R_2)=\frac25.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P(R_1\mid R_2)
=
\frac{\frac{13}{100}}{\frac25}
=
\frac{13}{100}\cdot \frac52
=
\frac{13}{40}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{P(\text{first ball red}\mid \text{second ball red})=\frac{13}{40}.}
\]

---

## (4) \(P(\text{sampled with replacement}\mid Y=2)\)

We want

\[
P(H\mid Y=2)
=
\frac{P(Y=2\mid H)P(H)}{P(Y=2)}.
\]

From above,

\[
P(Y=2\mid H)=\frac4{25},
\qquad
P(H)=\frac12,
\qquad
P(Y=2)=\frac{13}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[
P(H\mid Y=2)
=
\frac{\frac4{25}\cdot \frac12}{\frac{13}{100}}
=
\frac{\frac2{25}}{\frac{13}{100}}
=
\frac2{25}\cdot \frac{100}{13}
=
\frac8{13}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{P(\text{sampled with replacement}\mid Y=2)=\frac8{13}.}
\]
